summary: Defines a template for the QSPEC object, which carries QoS model specific information in the QoS NSLP, and a set of QSPEC parameters. They provide a common language across models like IntServ or Diffserv. It is an Experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: A form with common boxes for describing the service you want, which many different systems can read.

questions: how does qspec encode qos requirements
how do qspec parameters travel across domain boundaries
subtitle: A template for QoS parameters in network signaling.

tldr.problem: QoS NSLP needs a way to carry QoS requirements across different network domains that use different QoS models (IntServ, Diffserv, etc.), but each model uses different terminology and parameters.
tldr.mechanism: QSPEC defines a common template with a set of reusable parameters like traffic model, latency, loss ratio, and priorities that can express QoS requirements independent of the underlying QoS model.
tldr.outcome: Domains can interoperate even when they support different QoS models by translating between their local QoS models and the common QSPEC parameters.

today: RFC 5975 is an Experimental protocol and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the core QSPEC template that QoS NSLP depends on for carrying QoS requirements across different network domains.

sections.title: What QSPEC Is and Why It Matters
sections.content:
The QoS NSLP (QoS NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol) is used to signal QoS reservations across a network path. However, different network domains may use different QoS models (QOSMs) to deliver service, such as IntServ (which reserves resources for individual flows) or Diffserv (which marks packets with priority levels). Each model has its own terminology and parameters.

RFC 5975 solves this problem by defining the QSPEC, a common template and set of parameters that travels inside QoS NSLP messages. The QSPEC encapsulates all QoS-specific information in a way that QoS NSLP itself remains agnostic to the specific model in use. Each domain can translate the common QSPEC parameters into its local QoS model and back.

The Initiator QSPEC is created by the originating node (the QNI, or QoS NSIS Initiator) and travels end-to-end. Intermediate nodes may also create a Local QSPEC that describes resources in their domain while encapsulating the Initiator QSPEC, ensuring that end-to-end intent is preserved.
sections.eli5: QSPEC is a form you fill out at the start of your request that says what kind of service you need. Every network along the path can read this form and tell you if they can deliver it.

sections.title: The Structure of a QSPEC
sections.content:
A QSPEC is made up of QSPEC objects, each of which contains a set of QSPEC parameters. The template defines four main QSPEC objects:

  • QoS Desired: Describes the resources the initiator requests. This is a read-only object in messages; its parameters may not be overwritten.
  • QoS Available: Describes resources currently available along the path. Each node updates this object (reducing values if needed) to reflect what it can provide, making it a read-write object. By the time it reaches the receiver, it shows the bottleneck resources on the path.
  • QoS Reserved: Describes the resources actually reserved. It appears in response messages and reflects what was agreed to.
  • Minimum QoS: Specifies the minimum acceptable resources (unique to QSPEC, not found in RSVP). If QoS Available drops below these minimums, the reservation fails.

A given QSPEC message may contain only some of these objects. For example, a simple reservation request might include only QoS Desired, while a more detailed request might include QoS Desired, QoS Available (to collect path information), and Minimum QoS.
sections.eli5: A QSPEC is like a package with four possible sections: what you want, what you can get, what you're keeping, and what the minimum acceptable is. Not every package needs all sections.

sections.title: QSPEC Parameters
sections.content:
The QSPEC template includes a set of reusable parameters that can describe QoS in terms independent of any specific model. The Traffic Model (TMOD) parameter is mandatory; all others are optional:

  • Traffic Model: Describes the traffic characteristics using a token bucket with five sub-parameters: rate (r), bucket size (b), peak rate (p), minimum policed unit (m), and maximum packet size (MPS). This lets the network understand how traffic will behave.
  • Path Parameters: Path Latency, Path Jitter, Path PLR (packet loss ratio), and Path PER (packet error ratio) are cumulative constraints. Each node adds its own contribution, and the accumulated value tells the receiver the end-to-end quality.
  • Priority Parameters: Preemption Priority (for new flows to preempt existing ones), Defending Priority (for existing flows to resist preemption), and Admission Priority (for emergency services) allow differentiation of traffic importance.
  • Traffic Handling: The Excess Treatment parameter tells nodes how to handle traffic that exceeds the TMOD (drop, shape, or re-mark it).
  • Classification: PHB Class and DSTE Class Type allow specification of how traffic should be marked or classified in Diffserv or MPLS environments.

The Initiator QSPEC may flag a parameter as mandatory (M flag set) to indicate that all nodes must interpret it or the reservation fails. Parameters without the M flag may be interpreted by nodes that support them but can be safely ignored by others.
sections.eli5: Parameters are like details on the form: how fast your traffic goes, how much delay you can accept, how important it is, and how the network should treat packets that go over the limit.

sections.title: How Nodes Process QSPEC Messages
sections.content:
When a RESERVE message carrying a QSPEC travels through the network, each QNE (QoS NSIS Entity) processes it according to the message sequence and object combination. RFC 5975 defines three message sequences:

  • Two-Way Transactions: QNI sends a RESERVE; QNR responds with a RESPONSE. The QNI can include just QoS Desired, or also QoS Available and Minimum QoS to probe available resources.
  • Three-Way Transactions: Allows the QNR to query back toward the QNI before committing to a reservation.
  • Resource Queries: Allow exploration of available QoS without making a reservation.

Each node evaluates whether it can provide the requested QoS. If it can, it reserves resources. If it cannot, it sets an Error (E) flag on the failed parameter to indicate reservation failure. If it does not understand a parameter with the M flag set, it sets a Not Supported (N) flag and fails the reservation. When any node detects failure, it generates a RESPONSE message with an appropriate error code: 'Reservation Success', 'Reservation Failure', 'Malformed QSPEC', or 'Incompatible QSPEC'.

At a domain boundary, an ingress QNE may translate the Initiator QSPEC into a Local QSPEC (using the domain-specific parameters) while encapsulating the Initiator QSPEC, so interior nodes only see the Local QSPEC. The egress QNE then removes the Local QSPEC and forwards the Initiator QSPEC onward.
sections.eli5: Each node checks the form to see if it can deliver what's requested. If it can, it marks success. If not, it marks which part failed and sends word back to the start. Nodes can also translate the form into their own language for local use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
QSPEC security is directly tied to QoS NSLP security, as documented in RFC 5974. The key concern specific to QSPEC is the priority parameter, which opens the possibility of theft-of-service attacks. A malicious user could falsely claim emergency priority for their flows, preventing legitimate emergency calls (such as E911) from getting through.

The RFC notes several options for countering such attacks: restricting emergency priority to authorized user groups (such as police departments), or limiting which destination addresses can use emergency priority. These controls must be enforced at the network edge and in policy mechanisms, not in QSPEC itself. Network operators should implement these protections based on their threat model and regulatory environment.
sections.eli5: Someone could cheat by claiming their traffic is an emergency when it is not, blocking real emergencies. Networks have to set rules about who is allowed to say their traffic is urgent.
